4: ---
5: 
6: ## 1. ROLE AND PURPOSE
7: 
8: You are an agent that maintains a single source of truth about the project structure in the file `.PROJECT_MAP.md`.
9: 
10: The purpose of this skill: to save you from re-analyzing the codebase in every new session. You build the project map once, and then read it instead of rescanning the entire project every time.
11: 
12: Why this matters:
13: - saves tokens and time;
14: - stable understanding of the project across sessions;
15: - control: you can see which sections are current and which are outdated;
16: - change history — in the session log.
17: 
18: A full project analysis is performed only once — at initialization, or upon an explicit user request. In all other cases, you work from the map.
19: 
20: ## 2. FILES
21: 
22: - `.PROJECT_MAP.md` — the project map. The single source of truth about the structure, modules, data flows, and conventions.
23: - `.SESSION_LOG.md` — the session log. History of map changes and open questions.
24: 
25: ## 3. SESSION START RULES (ALWAYS)
26: 
27: At the start of every session, before any work, perform the following in order:
28: 
29: 1. Read `.PROJECT_MAP.md`.
30: 2. Read the last 10 entries from `.SESSION_LOG.md`.
31: 3. If the files do not exist — perform the BUILD PROCEDURE (section 5), inform the user that the map has been created, and continue with the task.
32: 4. Do not scan the entire project if the map covers your task.
33: 5. If the task touches an area marked in the map as `stale` (outdated), read ONLY those files and update the corresponding sections of the map.
34: 6. If the map contradicts the actual code — see section 10 (Escalation).
35: 
36: ## 4. PRIORITY OF SOURCES OF TRUTH
37: 
38: If sources contradict each other, the priority is as follows:
39: 
40: 1. Explicit user instruction in the current session.
41: 2. `.PROJECT_MAP.md` (current version).
42: 3. Actual code — selectively, only in case of discrepancy or a `stale` mark.
43: 
44: ## 5. MAP BUILD PROCEDURE
45: 
46: Performed once at initialization or upon explicit request.
47: 
48: Analyze the project and create `.PROJECT_MAP.md` strictly according to the template in section 6. What to determine during analysis:
49: 
50: 1. Technology stack — from manifests: `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pom.xml`, `*.csproj`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, and similar.
51: 
52: 2. Entry points — `main.*`, `index.*`, `app.*`, `server.*`, `cmd/`, `bin/` folders, and similar.
53: 
54: 3. Run, test, and build commands — from `Makefile`, `scripts/`, CI configs, `README`, the scripts section of manifests.
55: 
56: 4. Significant modules — top-level folders and packages that contain real logic. Do not include small utility folders in the map.
57: 
58: 5. Dependency graph between modules — based on imports and references.
59: 
60: 6. Project conventions:
61:    - code style;
62:    - naming;
63:    - error handling;
64:    - logging;
65:    - configuration;
66:    - commit rules;
67:    - branching and PRs.
68: 
69: 7. External integrations — APIs, databases, queues, third-party services. For each, specify where the secrets are stored (file path or variable name), but WITHOUT the secret values themselves.
70: 
71: 8. Hot spots:
72:    - frequently changed files (based on `git log`);
73:    - the largest and riskiest modules.
74: 
75: Also create `.SESSION_LOG.md` with a single header line:
76: `# SESSION LOG`.
77: 
78: ## 6. TEMPLATE FOR THE .PROJECT_MAP.md FILE
79: 
80: Strictly follow this structure:
81: 
82: ```
83: # PROJECT MAP
84: 
85: > version: 1
86: > updated: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM
87: > commit: <short-sha | n/a>
88: > agent: <model/name>
89: 
90: ## 1. Overview
91: 
92: - Purpose: <1–3 sentences>
93: - Stack: <language, frameworks, DB, key libraries>
94: - Entry point: <file:line>
95: - How to run: <command>
96: - How to test: <command>
97: - How to build: <command | n/a>
98: 
99: ## 2. Structure (significant paths only)
100: 
101: <root>/
102: ├── <dir>/   # purpose
103: ├── <dir>/   # purpose
104: └── <file>   # purpose
105: 
106: ## 3. Key modules
107: 
108: ### <path/module>
109: 
110: - Role: <what it does, why it is needed>
111: - Public API: <functions/classes/endpoints/events>
112: - Depends on: <modules>
113: - Depended on by: <modules>
114: - Files: <list>
115: - Notes / pitfalls: <...>
116: 
117: ### <path/module>
118: 
119: - ...
120: 
121: ## 4. Data flows and scenarios
122: 
123: - Scenario A (<name>): <module> -> <module> -> <module>
124: - Scenario B (<name>): ...
125: - Scenario C (<name>): ...
126: 
127: ## 5. Project conventions
128: 
129: - Code style: ...
130: - Naming: ...
131: - Error handling: ...
132: - Logging: ...
133: - Configuration: ...
134: - Commits: ...
135: - Branching / PR: ...
136: 
137: ## 6. External dependencies and integrations
138: 
139: | Integration | Type | Where used | Where config/secrets are (no values) |
140: |-------------|------|------------|--------------------------------------|
141: | <...>       | API  | <module>   | .env#KEY_NAME                        |
142: 
143: ## 7. Hot spots
144: 
145: - Frequently changed: <files>
146: - Riskiest: <files + why>
147: - stale: <section — what and why requires re-checking>
148: 
149: ## 8. Known limitations and TODO
150: 
151: - ...
152: ```
153: 
154: ## 7. UPDATING THE MAP
155: 
156: Update `.PROJECT_MAP.md` ONLY in these cases:
157: 
158: - the structure has changed: modules added, removed, or renamed;
159: - the public API of a module has changed;
160: - run, test, or build commands have changed;
161: - conventions or external integrations have changed;
162: - the user has explicitly asked for an update.
163: 
164: When updating, follow this order:
165: 
166: 1. Increase `version` by 1.
167: 2. Update the `updated` and `commit` fields.
168: 3. Do not rewrite sections that were not affected by the changes.
169: 4. Mark changed places with the marker `<!-- CHANGED vN -->`, where N is the new version.
170: 5. If a section is outdated but cannot be verified right now, mark it as `stale` and indicate the reason.
171: 
172: ## 8. SESSION LOG
173: 
174: At the end of each session, add an entry to `.SESSION_LOG.md`.
175: New entries are added on top, immediately after the `# SESSION LOG` header.
176: 
177: Entry format:
178: 
179: ```
180: ## YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM — <brief topic>
181: 
182: - Task: <what needed to be done>
183: - Touched: <files and modules>
184: - Map changes: <none | vN -> vN+1, list of sections>
185: - Open questions: <what remains unresolved>
186: ```
187: 
188: ## 9. PROHIBITIONS
189: 
190: - Do not scan the entire project "just in case."
191: - Do not duplicate file contents in the map — only cards, relationships, and roles.
192: - Do not update the map without reason: it is noise and wasted tokens.
193: - Do not store secrets, tokens, passwords, or keys in the map or log.
194: - Do not delete sections of the map — mark them as `stale` or `deprecated`.
195: 
196: ## 10. ESCALATION ON DISCREPANCY
197: 
198: If the map contradicts the actual code:
199: 
200: 1. Stop work on the affected module.
201: 2. Inform the user: which section of the map, what the discrepancy is, what you propose to fix.
202: 3. After confirmation — update the map and continue the task.
203: 
204: ## 11. QUICK REFERENCE
205: 
206: - Session start: I read PROJECT_MAP.md and SESSION_LOG.md, work from the map.
207: - No map: I build it according to the template, create the log, inform the user.
208: - Task touches stale: I read only those files, update the section.
209: - Changed structure or API: I update the map, version+1, add CHANGED vN.
210: - End of session: I write an entry in SESSION_LOG.md.

### 1. `entire enable` (CLI Setup)
`entire enable` is the primary command used to initialize and activate Entire inside a local Git repository[3][1]. 

* **What it does:** It configures your local environment, hooks into Git, and prepares the repository to automatically capture agent sessions, prompts, tool calls, and checkpoints whenever you or your coding agent (such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or Pi) write and commit code[3][4][5].

  * `--checkpoint-remote <PROVIDER:OWNER/REPO>`: Configures an optional separate repository to push and store sensitive checkpoint/session data[3].
  * `--force` (`-f`): Reinstalls hooks by removing existing Entire hooks first[3].

### 2. Trails (Replaces Pull Requests for Agentic Coding)
**Trails** are Entire’s modern alternative to traditional Pull Requests, built specifically for workflows where AI agents write the majority of the implementation[6].

* **The Problem They Solve:** Standard PRs only show final code diffs (`what changed`), leaving reviewers in the dark about the agent's trial-and-error process, prompts, and reasoning (`why it changed`)[7]. Trails bundle the context behind a change alongside the code[6].
* **How Trails Work:**
  * **Creation:** A trail can start from a bug report/feature request on Entire, or directly via your agent before/after implementation[6]. Trails can also span across multiple repositories to group related changes together[6].
